title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
This post replicates the headline difference-in-differences result from Card and Krueger (1994) using the original public fast-food restaurant data. The central finding is that employment at New Jersey restaurants did not fall relative to nearby Pennsylvania after New Jersey raised its minimum wage in April 1992.

In Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, David Card and Alan Krueger study whether New Jersey’s April 1, 1992 minimum-wage increase reduced employment in the fast-food sector. Their research design compares restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage rose from $4.25 to $5.05, with similar restaurants in eastern Pennsylvania, where the minimum wage remained unchanged.
The paper became influential because it challenged a simple textbook prediction: if the price of low-wage labor rises, employment should decline. Card and Krueger instead find no evidence of an employment loss. Their empirical strategy is a classic difference-in-differences design, comparing the change in employment in New Jersey before and after the policy to the contemporaneous change in Pennsylvania.
This post is organized to answer each part of the assignment directly:

It introduces the paper’s research question and empirical setting.
It replicates a key statistical finding from the paper, especially the Table 3 difference-in-differences estimate.
It goes beyond the core replication by reproducing another result, converting Table 3 into a figure, and explaining why the method supports a causal interpretation.


Local paper PDF: card_krueger_1994.pdf
Original data archive source: https://davidcard.berkeley.edu/data_sets.html

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Main Analysis

Loading the Original Data
The public dataset is a fixed-width file containing 410 restaurants. The key outcome is full-time-equivalent employment, defined as
\[
\text{FTE} = \text{full-time employees} + \text{managers} + 0.5 \times \text{part-time employees}.
\]
One coding choice is essential for matching the published results:

stores coded as permanently closed in wave 2 are assigned zero employment;
temporarily closed stores are treated as missing in the post period.

]

    "sheet", "chain", "co_owned", "state", "southj", "centralj", "northj",
    "pa1", "pa2", "shore", "ncalls", "empft", "emppt", "nmgrs", "wage_st",
    "inctime", "firstinc", "bonus", "pctaff", "meals", "open", "hrsopen",

    "firstin2", "special2", "meals2", "open2r", "hrsopen2", "psoda2", "pfry2",
    "pentree2", "nregs2", "nregs112"
]

ck["nj"] = ck["state"]
ck["fte"] = ck["empft"] + ck["nmgrs"] + 0.5 * ck["emppt"]
ck["fte2_raw"] = ck["empft2"] + ck["nmgrs2"] + 0.5 * ck["emppt2"]

ck.loc[ck["status2"] == 3, "fte2_t3"] = 0

Replicating Table 4, Column (i)
Table 4 moves from raw mean differences to a regression framework. Column (i) regresses the change in employment on an indicator for New Jersey using a restricted sample: stores with valid employment changes and valid wage information in both waves, plus stores that permanently closed.
This restriction matters. The authors’ original SAS program constructs a sample of 357 stores for this specification, and using that same rule is what allows the replication to line up cleanly.

    ck["demp"].notna() & ((ck["closed"] == 1) | ((ck["closed"] == 0) & ck["dwage"].notna()))
].copy()

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Something Additional

Turn Table 3 into a Figure
To make the identification strategy easier to read, I translate Table 3 into a cleaner figure. The left panel shows average employment levels before and after the policy with standard-error bars. The right panel shows the within-state changes and the implied difference-in-differences estimate.









The figure makes the identifying comparison immediate: employment edges up in New Jersey, falls in Pennsylvania, and the gap between those two changes is the treatment effect.


Why Difference-in-Differences Supports a Causal Interpretation
The logic of difference-in-differences is straightforward. New Jersey and Pennsylvania may differ for many fixed reasons, and 1992 may have brought broader shocks that affected both states. The estimator removes both sources of variation:
\[
\text{Effect} =
(\overline{Y}_{NJ,after} - \overline{Y}_{NJ,before})
-
(\overline{Y}_{PA,after} - \overline{Y}_{PA,before}).
\]
Under the parallel trends assumption, Pennsylvania provides a credible estimate of how employment in New Jersey would have changed even without the policy. The remaining difference is then interpreted as the effect of the minimum-wage increase.
The same idea can be written as a regression:
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha + \beta_1 NJ_i + \beta_2 Post_t + \beta_3 (NJ_i \times Post_t) + \varepsilon_{it},
\]
where \(\beta_3\) is the difference-in-differences estimate.

panel = pd.concat([
    ck[["sheet", "nj", "fte"]].rename(columns={"fte": "employment"}).assign(post=0),
    ck[["sheet", "nj", "fte2_t3"]].rename(columns={"fte2_t3": "employment"}).assign(post=1)
], ignore_index=True)

panel = panel.dropna(subset=["employment"])
did_model = smf.ols("employment ~ nj * post", data=panel).fit()

did_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Coefficient": ["Interaction: nj x post"],
    "Estimate": [did_model.params["nj:post"]],
    "Standard error": [did_model.bse["nj:post"]]
})

show_table(did_table, "Difference-in-differences regression equivalent to the Table 3 comparison", precision=3)

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Conclusion
This replication reproduces the central empirical pattern in Card and Krueger (1994). The selected descriptive statistics from Table 2 line up closely, the Table 3 difference-in-differences estimate matches at 2.75, and the Table 4 column (i) regression yields the same substantive result on the restricted sample.
The substantive conclusion is also the same as in the original paper: in this setting, the New Jersey minimum-wage increase does not appear to have reduced fast-food employment relative to nearby Pennsylvania. That result is what makes the paper so memorable. It shows how a simple but well-executed research design can overturn an intuitive prediction and reshape an important policy debate.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
Suppose my website has a place where visitors can sign up for a newsletter. I want to test which of two calls to action gets more sign ups.

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

I can study this with an A/B test. In an A/B test, visitors are randomly shown one version or the other, and then I compare the sign-up rates in the two groups.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
Suppose my website has a place where visitors can sign up for a newsletter. I want to test which of two calls to action gets more sign ups.

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

I can study this with an A/B test. In an A/B test, visitors are randomly shown one version or the other, and then I compare the sign-up rates in the two groups.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up or does not sign up, so each outcome is Bernoulli. Let \(\pi_A\) be the sign-up probability for CTA A and let \(\pi_B\) be the sign-up probability for CTA B.
The quantity I care about is
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B,
\]
which is the difference in sign-up rates.
I estimate this with the difference in sample means:
\[
\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B.
\]
Because the data are 0s and 1s, each sample mean is just a sample proportion.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
Simulating Data
In real life, I would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\). For this exercise, I set them myself so I can compare my estimates to the truth.
I will use \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), so the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\). Then I simulate 1,000 observations for each group.

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n_A = 1000
n_B = 1000
true_theta = pi_A - pi_B

a = rng.binomial(1, pi_A, n_A)
b = rng.binomial(1, pi_B, n_B)

theta_hat = a.mean() - b.mean()

sim_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Group": ["CTA A", "CTA B", "Difference"],
    "Estimate": [a.mean(), b.mean(), theta_hat],
    "True value": [pi_A, pi_B, true_theta]
})
show_table(sim_table, "Simulated sign-up rates and the true values")

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers says that as the sample size gets larger, the sample mean gets closer to the population mean. That means \(\hat\theta\) should get closer to the true \(\theta\) when the sample is large.
To show this, I take the element-wise differences between the A and B draws and compute the running average.

diff = a - b
running_mean = np.cumsum(diff) / np.arange(1, len(diff) + 1)










At first the running average moves around a lot. As more observations are included, it settles down near 0.04. This is what the Law of Large Numbers predicts.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Next, I want to know how precise my estimate is. The bootstrap helps with this. I resample the observed data with replacement many times, compute the difference in means each time, and use the standard deviation of those bootstrap estimates as the bootstrap standard error.

B = 1000
boot = np.empty(B)

for i in range(B):
    a_star = rng.choice(a, size=n_A, replace=True)
    b_star = rng.choice(b, size=n_B, replace=True)
    boot[i] = a_star.mean() - b_star.mean()

boot_se = boot.std(ddof=1)
pi_hat_A = a.mean()
pi_hat_B = b.mean()
analytic_se = np.sqrt(pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n_A + pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n_B)
ci_low = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
ci_high = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se

bootstrap_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Result": ["Bootstrap SE", "Analytical SE", "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper"],
    "Value": [boot_se, analytic_se, ci_low, ci_high]
})
show_table(bootstrap_table, "Bootstrap uncertainty summary")

text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem says that for large samples, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately Normal. The same idea applies to the difference in sample means.
To show this, I simulate 1,000 estimates of \(\hat\theta\) for four sample sizes: 25, 50, 100, and 500.









For small samples, the histograms look rough. As the sample size increases, they become smoother and more bell-shaped. This is the Central Limit Theorem in action.

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now I test the null hypothesis
\[
H_0: \theta = 0
\]
against the alternative
\[
H_1: \theta \neq 0.
\]
I use the test statistic
\[
z = \frac{\hat\theta}{SE(\hat\theta)}.
\]
By the Central Limit Theorem, this statistic is approximately standard Normal under the null. That is why I can use it to compute a p-value.
This is often called a t-test in practice, but here it is closer to a z-test because the data are Bernoulli and the Normal approximation comes from the CLT.

z_stat = theta_hat / analytic_se
p_value = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))

hypothesis_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Result": ["Estimate", "Standard error", "z statistic", "p-value"],
    "Value": [theta_hat, analytic_se, z_stat, p_value]
})
show_table(hypothesis_table, "Hypothesis test results")

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
This same test can be written as a regression. I stack the two groups into one dataset with an outcome \(Y_i\) and an indicator \(D_i\) that equals 1 for CTA A and 0 for CTA B.
Then I estimate
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i.
\]
Here, \(\beta_0\) is the mean of group B, and \(\beta_1\) is the difference between group A and group B. So \(\beta_1 = \theta\).

ab = pd.DataFrame({
    "y": np.concatenate([a, b]),
    "D": np.concatenate([np.ones(n_A), np.zeros(n_B)])
})

X = sm.add_constant(ab["D"])
model = sm.OLS(ab["y"], X).fit()

regression_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Result": ["beta_1", "Standard error", "t statistic", "p-value"],
    "Value": [model.params["D"], model.bse["D"], model.tvalues["D"], model.pvalues["D"]]
})

title: MGTA-495 HW1: A/B Testing and Simulating Key Ideas in Frequentist Statistical Inference
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Peeking is a problem in frequentist statistics because each extra test gives another chance for a false positive. A single test at the 5% level has a 5% false positive rate, but checking many times raises the chance of rejecting the null by mistake.
To show this, I simulate a world where the null is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\). I test after every 100 observations per group and record whether any of the 10 tests is significant.

peek_sizes = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)
false_positive = []

for _ in range(10000):
    a0 = rng.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    b0 = rng.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    reject = False

    for n in peek_sizes:
        diff_n = a0[:n].mean() - b0[:n].mean()
        se_n = np.sqrt(a0[:n].mean() * (1 - a0[:n].mean()) / n + b0[:n].mean() * (1 - b0[:n].mean()) / n)
        if se_n == 0:
            continue
        z_n = diff_n / se_n
        p_n = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_n)))
        if p_n < 0.05:
            reject = True
            break

    false_positive.append(reject)

peek_rate = np.mean(false_positive)

peeking_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Procedure": ["Single test", "Peeking every 100"],

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Every invention starts as an idea. When engineers and scientists create something new, they can file for a patent: an official document from the government granting them the exclusive right to their invention. Patents protect ideas from being copied, and winning one can be extremely valuable for an engineering firm. But the application process is long, technical, and highly competitive.
Blueprinty is a small company that builds software specifically for preparing patent applications. Think of it like a specialized assistant that helps engineering firms write stronger, more complete submissions. Blueprinty’s marketing team wants to make a bold claim: firms that use their software get more patents approved than firms that don’t.
That sounds easy to check. Just compare the two groups, right? Here’s the catch.
Imagine you noticed that kids who own expensive sports equipment tend to win more trophies. Does the equipment make them win? Maybe. Or maybe kids who are already talented athletes are more likely to buy expensive equipment in the first place. The equipment might just be a marker of who’s already good, not the reason they win.
The same problem applies here. Blueprinty’s customers are not a random sample of engineering firms. Companies that invest in specialized patent software are probably already more focused on patents, better-funded, and more experienced with the application process. Any difference in patent counts might reflect who those firms already are, not what the software does for them.
Blueprinty collected data on 1,500 mature (non-startup) engineering firms. For each firm, we know how many patents it was awarded over the last five years, which region it operates in, how long it has been incorporated, and whether it uses Blueprinty’s software. The ideal study would track each firm before and after adopting the software, measuring the change directly. That data does not exist. Instead, we have a single snapshot of 1,500 firms at one point in time.
To get a fair estimate of the Blueprinty effect, we need to compare firms that are similar in age and region, and then ask whether customers still outperform. That is exactly what Poisson regression estimated by maximum likelihood lets us do.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Exploring the Data

Do Customers Win More Patents?
The simplest question first: do Blueprinty customers actually have higher patent counts? The chart below compares the full distributions side by side on the same scale. Hover over any bar to see the exact counts.


                                                    


Customers average np.float64(4.13) patents over five years, compared to np.float64(3.47) for non-customers: a gap of np.float64(0.66) patents. Both distributions are right-skewed, meaning most firms earn just a few patents while a small number earn many. This is a classic pattern for count data. The gap looks meaningful, but before crediting the software, we need to check whether the two groups are actually comparable on other dimensions.


Who Uses Blueprinty?
To answer that, we compare customers and non-customers on two dimensions that could independently affect patent outcomes: region and firm age.









Nearly 68% of Blueprinty’s customers are in the Northeast, versus only about 27% of non-customers. The Midwest, South, and Northwest are sharply underrepresented among customers. The Northeast is home to dense networks of research universities, technology companies, and patent lawyers, all of which can boost patent success independent of any software. A simple comparison of the two groups would confuse this geographic advantage with a software advantage. This is why we cannot just compare group averages and stop there: a model that controls for region is needed to separate the software effect from the location effect.









Customers are also systematically younger: they average np.float64(26.9) years old versus np.float64(26.1) years for non-customers. Firm age can push patent counts in either direction. Younger firms may be in faster-growing fields with more to innovate; older firms have had more years to file applications. Either way, the age imbalance means a direct comparison of the two groups is also comparing younger firms to older firms, not just software users to non-users. Controlling for age is essential before we can say anything about Blueprinty specifically.
The takeaway: customers and non-customers differ in region and age, not just software use. To isolate the Blueprinty effect, we need a model that holds those differences constant. That is the task of the sections that follow.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood

Why Poisson?
Patent counts are whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, … A firm cannot win 2.7 patents, and it cannot win a negative number. Standard regression tools assume the outcome can be any real number, including negatives, which is a poor fit for count data.
The Poisson distribution was designed exactly for this situation. It describes the probability of seeing \(k\) events in a fixed time window, where events occur independently at a constant average rate. A single positive number, \(\lambda\), controls everything: it is both the mean and the variance of the distribution. We start with the simplest version of the model, where every firm shares the same patent rate \(\lambda\), and estimate it from the data.






NoteGoing Deeper: Deriving the Log-Likelihood



The Poisson probability mass function for a single observation \(Y\) is:
\[f(Y \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y}}{Y!}\]
Step 1: Joint likelihood for \(n\) independent observations.
If the \(n\) firms are independent draws from the same Poisson distribution, the probability of seeing all \(n\) outcomes at once is the product of the individual probabilities:
\[L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!} = e^{-n\lambda}\;\lambda^{\sum_i Y_i}\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{Y_i!}\]
Step 2: Take the log.
Products are hard to work with analytically. The natural log converts the product into a sum, which is far easier to differentiate and maximize:
\[\ell(\lambda) = \log L(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i\right)\log\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(Y_i!)\]
Step 3: Find the maximum analytically.
The last term does not depend on \(\lambda\), so it does not affect the location of the maximum. Taking the derivative and setting it to zero:
\[\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{\sum_i Y_i}{\lambda} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\lambda_{\text{MLE}} = \bar{Y}\]
The maximum likelihood estimate is the sample mean. This makes perfect intuitive sense: the mean of a Poisson distribution is \(\lambda\) itself, so the best estimate of \(\lambda\) given the data is just the observed average.




Coding the Log-Likelihood

def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    if lam <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - special.gammaln(Y + 1))



Watching the Optimizer Find the MLE
One of the best ways to understand maximum likelihood estimation is to watch the optimizer use the log-likelihood curve to find its answer. The animation below shows the full curve for a range of \(\lambda\) values, with a red dot representing the optimizer starting from a bad initial guess and climbing toward the peak. Press Play to watch the search in action.


                                                    


The red dot starts at \(\lambda = 0.7\), far from the true answer. Each step, the gradient tells it which direction to move (uphill on the curve). The steps shrink as it nears the top, and it settles at \(\bar{Y} \approx\) 3.685, the sample mean, exactly as the math predicts. The peak of the log-likelihood curve is the MLE: the single value of \(\lambda\) that makes the observed data most probable under the Poisson model.


Numerical Confirmation

result_scalar = optimize.minimize_scalar(
    lambda l: -poisson_loglikelihood(l, Y),
    bounds=(0.01, 20),
    method="bounded",
)
lambda_mle = result_scalar.x

print(f"Numerical MLE  : {lambda_mle:.6f}")
print(f"Sample mean Y  : {y_bar:.6f}")
print(f"Difference     : {abs(lambda_mle - y_bar):.2e}")

Numerical MLE  : 3.684667
Sample mean Y  : 3.684667
Difference     : 1.28e-07


The computer and the formula agree to six decimal places. Both methods solve the same problem: one with calculus, the other with a numerical search. Both lead to the sample mean, confirming that the MLE for a Poisson model is \(\hat\lambda = \bar{Y}\).

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression

Letting Each Firm Have Its Own Rate
The simple model assumed every firm has the same patent rate \(\lambda\). That is too coarse. A five-year-old Northeast firm and a thirty-year-old Midwest firm operate in very different environments and should have different expected rates. Poisson regression extends the model so each firm \(i\) gets its own rate \(\lambda_i\), determined by its own characteristics:
\[Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \qquad\text{where}\qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i^\prime\beta)\]
Why the exponential? The formula \(X_i^\prime\beta\) is a weighted combination of the firm’s features and can be any real number, including negatives. But \(\lambda_i\) must be strictly positive (a negative patent rate makes no sense). Applying the exponential maps any real number onto a positive value, solving the constraint cleanly. The coefficients \(\beta\) are still estimated by maximum likelihood.


Building the Design Matrix

regions  = ["Midwest", "Northwest", "South", "Southwest"]   # Northeast = reference
age_mean = df["age"].mean()
age_dm   = df["age"] - age_mean   # mean-centered age

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "intercept"   : 1,
    "age"         : age_dm,
    "age_sq"      : age_dm ** 2,
    **{f"region_{r}": (df["region"] == r).astype(int) for r in regions},
    "iscustomer"  : df["iscustomer"],
})
X_mat = X.values.astype(float)
Y_vec = df["patents"].values.astype(float)

The matrix \(X\) contains one column for each predictor:

Intercept: sets the baseline for a Northeast firm of average age that does not use Blueprinty.
Age (centered): firm age shifted so that zero means “average age” (np.float64(26.4) years).
Age squared (centered): captures the curved relationship between age and patent rates.
Region dummies: one indicator for each of Midwest, Northwest, South, and Southwest. The Northeast is the reference category and is left out.
Customer indicator: 1 if the firm uses Blueprinty, 0 if not.







NoteGoing Deeper: Why Age Squared and Why Drop a Region?



Why include age squared? The relationship between firm age and patent productivity is unlikely to be a straight line. Young firms may be ramping up their R&D investment; mid-life firms may be at peak output; older firms may see declining returns as their core technologies mature. Adding \(\text{age}^2\) lets the model fit this curve. Without it, the model would assume each additional year of age always changes the patent rate by the same fixed amount, regardless of how old the firm already is.
Why drop one region? If we included all five regions as indicator columns, those five columns would sum to 1 for every firm, which is identical to the intercept column (also all 1s). This perfect collinearity makes it impossible for the optimizer to separately identify the intercept and all five regional effects simultaneously. The fix is to drop one region (we drop Northeast) and treat it as the baseline. Every other region’s coefficient then represents the difference in log-rate relative to the Northeast.




Updated Log-Likelihood

def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    eta = np.clip(X @ beta, -30, 30)
    lam = np.exp(eta)
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - special.gammaln(Y + 1))



Finding the Best Coefficients

def neg_ll(beta, Y, X):
    return -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X)

beta_init = np.zeros(X_mat.shape[1])

result_reg = optimize.minimize(
    neg_ll, beta_init, args=(Y_vec, X_mat),
    method="BFGS",
    options={"maxiter": 50_000, "gtol": 1e-10},
)
beta_hat = result_reg.x



Computing Standard Errors
To know how confident we should be in each coefficient estimate, we need standard errors. These come from measuring how sharply the log-likelihood surface curves at its peak. A sharp, steep peak means the data pin down \(\hat\beta\) tightly (small standard errors). A flat, broad peak means many values of \(\beta\) fit nearly as well (large standard errors).






NoteGoing Deeper: The Hessian Formula for Standard Errors



The curvature of the log-likelihood surface is captured by the Hessian matrix \(H(\ell)\): the matrix of second derivatives evaluated at \(\hat\beta\). For Poisson regression, the Hessian has a clean analytical form:
\[H(\ell) = -X^\prime \,\mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda)\, X \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta) = \left(X^\prime \mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda) X\right)^{-1}\]
Standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal elements of \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)\). Using this analytical formula, rather than the numerical Hessian approximation that accumulates during BFGS optimization, yields exact standard errors that match built-in statistical software to five decimal places.



lam_hat  = np.exp(X_mat @ beta_hat)
H_loglik = -(X_mat * lam_hat[:, None]).T @ X_mat
cov_hat  = np.linalg.inv(-H_loglik)
se_hat   = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_hat))



Results at a Glance

A dot that does not cross the dashed zero line is statistically distinguishable from no effect. title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software

The Thought Experiment
A 23.1% boost in the patent rate does not directly answer the question “how many more patents does Blueprinty actually get me?” The answer depends on each firm’s baseline rate. A 23% boost means one extra patent for a firm that would otherwise get 4, but only about half an extra patent for a firm that would otherwise get 2.
To get a concrete number, we run a thought experiment using the fitted model:

Take every firm’s actual age and region. Set every firm’s customer status to 0 (non-customer). Predict each firm’s expected patents. Call this \(\hat{y}_0\).
Keep age and region the same. Set every firm’s customer status to 1 (customer). Predict each firm’s expected patents. Call this \(\hat{y}_1\).
Compute the average difference: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat{y}_{1i} - \hat{y}_{0i})\).

This average difference estimates what we would see, on average, if every firm in the dataset were to adopt Blueprinty, holding everything else equal.

X0 = X_mat.copy();  X0[:, -1] = 0   # everyone a non-customer
X1 = X_mat.copy();  X1[:, -1] = 1   # everyone a customer

y_hat0 = np.exp(X0 @ beta_hat)
y_hat1 = np.exp(X1 @ beta_hat)
diff   = y_hat1 - y_hat0
ate    = diff.mean()

print(f"Mean predicted patents, non-customer : {y_hat0.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Mean predicted patents, customer     : {y_hat1.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Average treatment effect (ATE)       : {ate:.4f}")

Mean predicted patents, non-customer : 3.4362
Mean predicted patents, customer     : 4.2290
Average treatment effect (ATE)       : 0.7928




Per-Firm Gain
Each dot below is one of the 1,500 firms in the dataset. The x-axis shows its predicted patent count in the non-customer scenario; the y-axis shows how many additional patents it would gain by adopting Blueprinty. Colors represent region. Hover over any firm to see its age, region, and estimated gain.


                                                    


Notice the upward slope in the chart: firms with higher baseline patent rates gain more patents in absolute terms when they adopt the software. This is a direct consequence of the multiplicative model. The same percentage boost translates to a larger absolute gain for more productive firms.


The Answer
Holding age and region fixed at each firm’s observed values, adopting Blueprinty is associated with 0.79 additional patents per firm over five years on average. For firms that average about 3.7 patents total, that is a meaningful gain: close to one full extra patent per five-year window.






NoteGoing Deeper: What This Establishes (and What It Doesn’t)



This is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. Firms chose whether to use Blueprinty; we did not assign them randomly. That matters because firms that adopt the software may differ from non-adopters in ways we cannot measure: the size of the legal department, how much the firm invests in R&D, how aggressively management pursues patents, and so on.
If these unobserved characteristics both make a firm more likely to adopt Blueprinty and more likely to win patents, our estimate would be biased upward. We would be giving the software credit for outcomes that are really a reflection of the type of firm that adopts it.
A credible causal claim would require one of the following:

A randomized experiment: randomly assign some firms to use the software and others not to, then compare outcomes.
A natural experiment: find an external event that caused some firms to adopt Blueprinty for reasons unrelated to their underlying patent capability.

Without one of these designs, the estimate of 0.79 additional patents is best interpreted as evidence consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim, not as proof of causation.


The results are consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim: after controlling for age and region, customers file more patents. Because firms self-select into using the software, however, unobserved differences between the two groups cannot be fully ruled out as an alternative explanation.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Picture this: a fellow MSBA student asks you to rate each of your 10 core classes on a scale of 1 to 10. You want to be honest, but you also don’t want to seem ungrateful or lazy. So everything gets an 8 or 9. The result? A pile of nearly identical numbers that tells absolutely nothing about what you actually prefer.
This is a real problem in survey research, and smart people have come up with a clever solution: MaxDiff, also called Best-Worst Scaling.
Instead of rating each class in isolation, MaxDiff puts you in a series of small competitions. On each screen you see four classes and answer two questions: “Which of these would you most want to take?” and “Which would you least want?” You do this eight times, each time with a different combination of four classes. Because you’re making real trade-offs under scarcity rather than assigning abstract numbers, the resulting data is much richer and more honest.

Think of it like a mini tournament. Every time a class wins (gets picked as best) or loses (gets picked as worst), it earns or loses points. By the end, the rankings emerge naturally from the competition results.

We ran exactly this survey with our MSBA cohort across all 10 core classes. Now we have real choice data, and we’re going to analyze it three different ways, each a bit more sophisticated than the last:

text:
Counts Analysis
Let’s start simple. The counts score for each class answers one question: when a class showed up, did students want it or avoid it?
\[\text{score}_j = \frac{\text{times chosen as best}}{\text{times shown}} - \frac{\text{times chosen as worst}}{\text{times shown}}\]
Reading the score is easy: - Score close to +1: Students almost always picked this class as their favorite when it appeared. A crowd favorite. - Score close to -1: Students almost always ranked this class last. Tough crowd. - Score close to 0: The class is middle of the pack, or students are split on it.
The counts approach is fast, honest, and needs zero modeling assumptions. You can explain it to anyone in under a minute. Its one weakness: it doesn’t account for who else was on screen. A class that kept getting shown against the two most popular classes will look worse than it really is. That’s exactly what the MNL model fixes. But for now, let’s see what the raw data tells us.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
The counts score is a great starting point, but it’s missing something important. Imagine a class that keeps getting shown alongside the two most popular classes in the survey. It’s always going to look bad by comparison, even if it would crush a different set of competitors. The counts approach can’t tell the difference.
The multinomial logit (MNL) model can. It models the actual probability of each pick, given exactly who was on screen at the time.
The MNL assigns each class \(j\) a utility \(\beta_j\). When a task shows items \(\{a, b, c, d\}\), the probability that item \(b\) is picked as best uses the softmax formula:
\[P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}\]
After the best is removed, the worst is picked from the remaining three using negated utilities (because the worst pick goes to the least preferred item):
\[P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}\]
So each 4-item task yields two observations: one MNL choice from the full set (best) and one from the reduced set of 3 (worst).
A note on identifiability: the softmax is unchanged if you add any constant to all betas. We cannot estimate unique values for all 10 betas without a normalization. The convention here is to fix \(\beta_1 = 0\) and estimate the remaining nine betas relative to class 1 (AI Math and Prog). Positive estimates mean “more preferred than AI Math,” negative means “less preferred.”
The chart below shows how the softmax formula translates utility values into pick probabilities. Try to build the intuition: a class with utility 2 is not twice as likely to be picked as a class with utility 1. The relationship is exponential.


                        
                                            


Class D has a utility of 2 – four times higher than Class A’s -1 in raw numbers. But through the softmax it wins 64% of choices vs Class A’s 3%. The MNL captures this nonlinear relationship precisely, which is something a simple count of wins and losses cannot do.


Show code
# Build one row per task: which items were shown, which was best, which was worst
task_rows = []
for (resp, task), grp in df_main.groupby(["respondent", "task"]):
    grp_sorted = grp.sort_values("position")
    items = grp_sorted["item"].tolist()
    best  = grp_sorted.loc[grp_sorted["response"] ==  1, "item"].values
    worst = grp_sorted.loc[grp_sorted["response"] == -1, "item"].values
    if len(best) == 1 and len(worst) == 1:
        task_rows.append({
            "respondent": resp, "task": task,
            "items": items,
            "best": int(best[0]), "worst": int(worst[0])
        })

task_df = pd.DataFrame(task_rows)

# Pre-compute arrays for vectorized likelihood
items_mat = np.array(task_df["items"].tolist(), dtype=int)  # (n_tasks, 4)
best_arr  = task_df["best"].values                           # (n_tasks,)
worst_arr = task_df["worst"].values                          # (n_tasks,)

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood
The log-likelihood sums over every task, collecting the log-probability of both the best and worst picks:
\[\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \Bigg[ \underbrace{\beta_{j^*_b} - \log \!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown}}\!\!\! \exp(\beta_j)}_{\text{best pick}} - \underbrace{\beta_{j^*_w} + \log \!\!\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}}\!\!\!\!\! \exp(-\beta_j)}_{\text{worst pick}} \Bigg]\]
The code below implements this in a vectorized form. Rather than looping over tasks, we use NumPy array indexing to compute all utilities at once, and scipy.special.logsumexp for numerical stability.


Show code
def ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr):
    """
    Log-likelihood of the MaxDiff MNL model.
    beta_free: length-9 array (beta_2 through beta_10; beta_1 = 0 is reference)
    """
    beta = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_free])  # beta[0] = 0 for item 1

    # Utilities for all shown items (n_tasks x 4)
    # items_mat has values 1-10; convert to 0-indexed
    u = beta[items_mat - 1]                      # shape (n_tasks, 4)

    # Best pick: util(best) - log(sum(exp(utils)))
    u_best       = beta[best_arr - 1]            # shape (n_tasks,)
    log_norm_best = logsumexp(u, axis=1)         # numerically stable
    lp_best      = u_best - log_norm_best

    # Worst pick: -util(worst) - log(sum(exp(-utils)) for remaining 3 items)
    # Trick: sum over all 4, then subtract the best item's contribution
    sum_neg_all    = np.exp(logsumexp(-u, axis=1))
    sum_neg_remain = np.maximum(sum_neg_all - np.exp(-u_best), 1e-300)
    lp_worst       = -beta[worst_arr - 1] - np.log(sum_neg_remain)

    return float(np.sum(lp_best + lp_worst))




Show code
def neg_ll(beta_free):
    return -ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr)

result = minimize(
    neg_ll,
    x0     = np.zeros(9),
    method = "BFGS",
    options= {"maxiter": 1000, "gtol": 1e-8}
)

beta_mle_free = result.x
beta_mle_full = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_mle_free])   # full 10-vector

# Standard errors from inverse Hessian (BFGS approximation)
se_free = np.sqrt(np.diag(result.hess_inv))
se_full = np.concatenate([[np.nan], se_free])

# Shares of preference: exp(beta) / sum(exp(beta))
shares_mle = np.exp(beta_mle_full) / np.exp(beta_mle_full).sum()

print(f"Optimizer converged: {result.success}  |  "
      f"Log-likelihood at MLE: {-result.fun:.2f}")

text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
Maximum likelihood gives us a single best guess for each beta, plus a standard error. That’s useful, but it’s just one number. Bayesian estimation goes further: instead of one answer, it gives us a full probability distribution over every possible value of each beta.
Why does that matter? Because we often care about derived quantities like shares of preference. Shares are a nonlinear transformation of the betas, so their uncertainty is tricky to compute from MLE alone (it requires an approximation called the delta method). With Bayesian MCMC, we can just push every sample through the share formula and take percentiles directly. No approximation needed.
The framework is Bayes’ rule applied to model parameters:
\[\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \text{data}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})\]
The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. We use a weakly informative prior: each free beta gets an independent normal prior centered at 0 with standard deviation \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16\). This is diffuse enough that the data, not the prior, drives the estimates.
Since we cannot sample from the posterior analytically, we use the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The idea: start somewhere in parameter space, propose a random step, accept or reject based on the ratio of posterior densities, and repeat thousands of times. The accepted draws trace out the posterior distribution.


Show code
def log_prior(beta_free):
    return np.sum(stats.norm.logpdf(beta_free, loc=0, scale=np.sqrt(10)))

def log_post(beta_free):
    return ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr) + log_prior(beta_free)

def mh_sampler(log_post_fn, beta0, n_iter, step, seed=123):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    K       = len(beta0)
    draws   = np.zeros((n_iter, K))
    beta    = beta0.copy()
    lp      = log_post_fn(beta)
    n_accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_prop = beta + np.random.normal(0, step, K)
        lp_prop   = log_post_fn(beta_prop)

        if np.log(np.random.uniform()) < lp_prop - lp:
            beta     = beta_prop
            lp       = lp_prop
            n_accept += 1

        draws[t] = beta

    return draws, n_accept / n_iter

print(f"Acceptance rate: {accept_rate:.1%}  (target: 25-40%)")

What Bayes adds over MLE: honest uncertainty on every number we care about. The credible intervals on shares are computed by pushing 15,000 posterior draws through the softmax formula and taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. No approximation, no delta method. With MLE you only get a point estimate plus a standard error on the beta; the uncertainty on the share itself requires extra work. Bayes gives it to you for free.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion

What did we find?
The answer is surprisingly clear: MSBA students want the career-focused, applied analytics courses. Customer Analytics and Marketing Analytics sit at the top of every ranking by a comfortable margin. These are the classes where you learn techniques you can use in a job interview or on day one of a new role.
The Capstone landing near the bottom is interesting. It is arguably the most valuable experience in the program in hindsight, but the preference data suggests that students anticipate it with more anxiety than excitement. An open-ended project with an external client is intimidating before it starts. Business Intelligence systems similarly ranks low, perhaps because it is perceived as more technical-infrastructure than analytics-application.


Pick the right tool for the job
All three methods told the same big story. But they have different strengths depending on what you need:






Note



Method Cheat Sheet







If you need…
Use…




A quick summary you can explain in 30 seconds
Counts analysis


A rigorous point estimate with classical standard errors
MLE MNL


Honest uncertainty on derived quantities like market shares
Bayesian MNL


Individual-level preference estimates (future work)
Hierarchical Bayes







Caveats
This survey was conducted on one cohort of self-selected MSBA students. Preferences almost certainly shift as students progress through the program – a first-year student who has not yet taken Capstone will rank it differently than someone who just finished it. Item presentation order can also influence responses: a class that appears early in the survey may be evaluated differently than one that shows up repeatedly at the end. Prior coursework outside the MSBA, current program standing, and career concentration all likely shape preferences in ways our model cannot separate. These results are a snapshot of one group at one point in time, and should not be treated as universal truths about MSBA preferences.


What comes next?
The most exciting extension is the hierarchical (mixed) logit model. Instead of one set of betas for the whole cohort, we would estimate a distribution over student-level betas. That model could answer questions like: “Do students with engineering backgrounds prefer methods courses while business students prefer application courses?” or “Is there a cluster of students who consistently disagree with the majority?” The Bayesian MCMC framework we built here is the natural foundation for that richer analysis.

section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices






Note




Before fitting an MNL, explain to the reader how the MaxDiff survey data converts into MNL choice observations. Reference the conjoint/MNL slides from week 5.
The MNL model assigns each item \(j\) a utility coefficient \(\beta_j\). On a task showing items \(\{a, b, c, d\}\), the probability that item \(b\) is picked best is the soft-max:

\[
P(\text{best} = b) \;=\; \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}
\]

The probability that item \(c\) is then picked worst — from the remaining 3 items, with utilities flipped — is:

\[
P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) \;=\; \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}
\]
So each task gives two MNL observations: the best-pick from the full set, and the worst-pick from the remaining set.

Identifiability: the soft-max is invariant to adding a constant to every \(\beta\), so only \(J - 1 = 9\) of the 10 coefficients are identified. Fix one as the reference — for example, set \(\beta_1 = 0\) and estimate \(\beta_2, \ldots, \beta_{10}\). Mention this normalization to the reader.
Reshape the data into a form convenient for the likelihood. One workable structure: for each task, store the 4 item numbers, which one was picked best, and which one was picked worst. You’ll iterate over tasks in the likelihood function.

text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood






Note




Write down the log-likelihood. Summing over \(N \cdot T\) tasks:

\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \;=\; \sum_{\text{tasks}} \Big[\, \beta_{j^*_b} \;-\; \log \!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown}}\!\!\! \exp(\beta_j) \;-\; \beta_{j^*_w} \;-\; \log \!\!\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}}\!\!\!\! \exp(-\beta_j) \,\Big]
\]
where \(j^*_b\) is the item picked best in that task and \(j^*_w\) is the item picked worst.

Code the log-likelihood as a function ll(beta, ...) where beta is a vector of length 9 (or 10, with \(\beta_1\) pinned to 0 inside the function). Use log-sum-exp form (v - log(rowSums(exp(v)))) for numerical stability — see the week-5 slides on fitting MNL by hand.
Maximize the log-likelihood. In R:

out <- optim(par = rep(0, 9), fn = ll, ...,
             method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
             control = list(fnscale = -1))

Report the estimated \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and standard errors. SEs come from the inverse of the negative Hessian:

se <- sqrt(diag(solve(-out$hessian)))

Convert the \(\hat\beta\)’s into shares of preference for interpretability:

\[
\hat s_j \;=\; \frac{\exp(\hat\beta_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^{10} \exp(\hat\beta_k)}
\]
These shares are easier to read than raw \(\beta\)’s — they sum to 1 across items and answer the question, “if all 10 classes were on a single screen, what fraction of choices would each one get?”

Display a table of items with \(\hat\beta_j\), \(SE(\hat\beta_j)\), and \(\hat s_j\). Plot the shares in a horizontal bar chart, sorted from highest to lowest.

text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation






Note




Now fit the same MNL model by Bayesian methods. Reference the week-7 slides on Bayes’ rule and the random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler.
The posterior over \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is

\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \;\propto\; L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\]
Use a weakly informative multivariate normal prior: \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0},\; 10 \cdot I)\). (SD \(\approx 3.2\) on each \(\beta\) is plenty diffuse without being absurd.)

Code a random-walk Metropolis sampler. The skeleton is:

log_post <- function(beta) ll(beta, ...) + sum(dnorm(beta, 0, sqrt(10), log = TRUE))

mh <- function(beta0, n_iter, step) {
  K <- length(beta0)
  draws <- matrix(NA, n_iter, K)
  beta  <- beta0
  lp    <- log_post(beta)
  accept <- 0
  for (t in 1:n_iter) {
    beta_star <- beta + rnorm(K, 0, step)
    lp_star   <- log_post(beta_star)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_star - lp) {
      beta <- beta_star; lp <- lp_star; accept <- accept + 1
    }
    draws[t, ] <- beta
  }
  list(draws = draws, accept_rate = accept / n_iter)
}

Run the sampler for ~20,000 iterations (or more if you have patience). Discard the first 25% as burn-in.
Tune the step size to land at an acceptance rate of roughly 25–40%. If acceptance is too low, halve the step; too high, double it. (See week-7 “Tuning the Step Size” slide.)
Run diagnostics: report the final acceptance rate, plot the trace for at least 2–3 of the \(\beta\) parameters (you should see a “fuzzy caterpillar,” not a slow drift), and confirm that the chain has stabilized after burn-in.
Compute and report:

Posterior mean \(\hat\beta_j\) for each item
95% credible interval \([2.5\%,\, 97.5\%]\) percentiles of the post-burn-in draws
Posterior shares of preference: for each MCMC draw, compute \(\hat s_j^{(s)} = \exp(\hat\beta_j^{(s)}) / \sum_k \exp(\hat\beta_k^{(s)})\), then take the posterior mean of the \(\hat s_j^{(s)}\) across draws.

Method 2 — MNL via Maximum Likelihood


The MNL knows who was on screen for every pick.

Best pick — softmax over 4 attributes:
\[P(\text{best} = j) = \frac{e^{\,\beta_j}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k \in \text{shown}} e^{\,\beta_k}}\]


Worst pick — from the remaining 3:

“If all 10 attributes appeared on one screen, what fraction of picks would each get?”

Attributes get credit / blame for competing against tough vs. weak opponents. It’s like strength-of-schedule adjustment.

Method 2 — MNL: Adding Competitive Context


The problem with counts: it ignores who else was on screen.
If “Winning” kept appearing against “Star Player” in the same tasks, both get penalized — even though they’d dominate against weaker alternatives.
The MNL fix: model the pick probability conditional on the exact set shown.
\[P(\text{most}=j) = \frac{e^{\beta_j}}{\sum_{k\in\text{shown}} e^{\beta_k}} \qquad P(\text{least}=j) = \frac{e^{-\beta_j}}{\sum_{k \neq \text{most}} e^{-\beta_k}}\]
We maximize the log-likelihood across all 800 tasks to get \(\hat\beta_j\) for each factor.


Shares of preference translate utilities into something actionable:
\[\text{share}_j = \frac{e^{\hat\beta_j}}{\sum_k e^{\hat\beta_k}}\]

“If all 10 factors were on one screen, what fraction of priority would each claim?”

Shares sum to 100% — making them a natural budget allocation guide.

The Strategic Takeaway


What the data says:


🏆 Winning + Star Player = 43% of all fan preference.
No promotion, fireworks show, or app feature competes with on-field performance. Marketing can’t fake its way around a losing team.




💰 Affordable tickets rank #3. If you can’t sign Ohtani, lower the ticket prices. Accessibility outperforms premium amenities every time.




📱 The mobile app ranks dead last. Teams spend millions on in-seat ordering tech. Fans care about it least of anything we tested.




Why three methods?
All three ranked the top 3 and bottom 3 identically — that’s what gives us confidence.
Differences only appeared in the competitive middle (giveaways vs. food vs. fireworks), where Bayesian credible intervals are widest and uncertainty is most honest.

The broader lesson:

MaxDiff doesn’t tell the marketing team what fans say they want. It reveals what they actually choose when forced to prioritize — and those are rarely the same thing.

WAR vs. Hierarchical Bayes

The Statistical Core




📊 WAR — Aggregate Logit


WAR_j = β̄₁·contact + β̄₂·power       + β̄₃·defense + β̄₄·age


β̄ = fixed league-average weights, applied identically to all 30 teams. A rebuilder and a contender get the exact same player valuation.


✗ 30 heterogeneous buyers treated as one homogeneous market




🧠 Hierarchical Bayes Conjoint


U_jt = β_1t·contact + β_2t·power      + β_3t·defense + β_4t·ageβ_t ~ N(β̄, Σ)


β_t = per-team weights, pooled toward the league mean but unique per team. Tampa Bay’s β ≠ New York’s β. HB recovers both simultaneously.


✓ Individual utility weights estimated for every buyer in the market




The HB prior β̄ is the league average — the WAR signal. The posterior β_t is each team’s true preference, regularized toward that mean.
